Sure. If you’re leaning toward **Notion**, the practical case is strongest when your project needs a **single structured system** for sources, notes, drafts, tasks, and timelines — especially if you want views and databases to do a lot of the organizing for you.

Here are the practical advantages of Notion for a solo 3-month research project:

---

## 1. Databases are ideal for source management

For research, one of the biggest organizational tasks is keeping track of sources. Notion’s databases are well suited to that.

You can build a **Source Database** with properties like:

- Title  
- Author  
- Year  
- Type: article, book, report, lecture, video, dataset, interview, etc.  
- Status: to read, reading, summarized, integrated, archived  
- Relevance level: primary, secondary, background  
- Topic tags  
- Date added  
- Date read  
- Citation  
- Notes summary  
- Links to related notes or draft sections  
- File attachments: PDFs, images, scans  
- Direct link to the original source  

Then you can switch between different views of the same data:

### Table view
Good for browsing and filtering sources.

### Gallery view
Useful if you attach PDFs or images and want to skim visually.

### Board view
Can work as a workflow:

- To Read
- Reading
- Summarized
- Integrated into Draft
- Archived

### Calendar view
Useful if you want to plan reading dates, draft deadlines, or review dates.

This is probably Notion’s biggest practical advantage here: you can manage your source library like a lightweight reference-management system without needing a separate tool.

---

## 2. You can create distinct but connected project areas

A research project usually involves more than just “notes.” Notion lets you build a workspace with separate sections that all share the same system.

A practical structure could be:

- **Home / Dashboard**
- **Source Library**
- **Notes / Ideas**
- **Literature Summary Log**
- **Drafts**
- **Tasks**
- **Timeline**
- **Research Questions**
- **Open Questions / Confusions**
- **Meetings / Labs / Field Notes**
- **Archive**

The advantage is that you can keep your project in one place without things becoming just a pile of loose files.

For example:

- A source in the **Source Library** can link to a summary note.
- A note in **Notes / Ideas** can link back to the source.
- A draft section can link to the relevant sources.
- A task can say “integrate source X into section Y.”
- The dashboard can show important deadlines.

That connected structure can be very helpful when your project grows.

---

## 3. Templates reduce repetitive setup

Notion has built-in templates, and you can also create your own. For a research project, templates are practical because you don’t want to recreate the same structure for every note, source, or draft section.

Useful templates might include:

### Source template
Fields for:

- Citation
- Core argument
- Method
- Key findings
- Limitations
- Relevance to your project
- Quotable passages
- Follow-up questions

### Note template
Fields for:

- Title
- Related sources
- Core idea
- Evidence
- Counterarguments
- Connections to other notes
- Questions to explore

### Draft page template
Fields for:

- Section heading
- Working thesis for that section
- Main points
- Supporting sources
- Evidence needed
- Revision notes
- Status

### Weekly review template
- What got done
- What is stuck
- What to focus on next week
- Deadlines coming up

This becomes really useful when you have many sources or notes and want consistency.

---

## 4. It works well as a project management layer

Notion isn’t just a note-taking tool; it’s also a lightweight project management tool. That can be useful for a 3-month project where you need to break things into steps.

You can have a **Task Database** with properties like:

- Task
- Status
- Due date
- Priority
- Related source
- Related draft section
- Effort estimate
- Notes

Then you can use filters to show:

- Tasks due this week
- High-priority tasks
- Tasks related to a specific source
- Tasks blocking the next draft milestone
- Completed tasks from last week

This is helpful if your research has multiple streams, for example:

- Literature review
- Data collection
- Interviews
- Analysis
- Drafting
- Revision
- References

Notion can keep all of those visible without depending on a separate task tracker.

---

## 5. Multiple views from one database are a real workflow advantage

One of Notion’s strongest features is that a single database can be viewed multiple ways.

For example, a **writing tasks** database can show:

- A board view by status:
  - Not started
  - In progress
  - Editing
  - Done

- A table view sorted by due date

- A calendar view showing deadlines

- A timeline view showing which sections you plan to work on each week

That means you don’t have to duplicate information. You can keep one centralized database and look at it depending on what you need.

For research, that can be very practical. Your source database, for example, can simultaneously be:

- A reading list
- A reference library
- A status tracker
- A citation index
- A research materials dashboard

---

## 6. It is good for consolidating different kinds of media

Notion handles more than just text. You can embed or attach:

- PDFs
- Images
- Diagrams
- Audio clips
- Videos
- YouTube links
- Tables
- Code blocks
- Callouts
- Toggles

That can be useful if your research involves:

- scanned documents
- lecture recordings
- images from fieldwork
- datasets
- screenshots
- diagrams
- quotations
- transcripts

Everything can live in the same page or database.

For example, a source page could have:

- A summary
- A citation
- A PDF attachment
- A transcript excerpt
- A quote bank
- A link to your draft section
- A list of follow-up questions

That is more integrated than having notes in one place, PDFs in another, and tasks in a third.

---

## 7. The free plan is likely sufficient

For a solo personal research project, Notion’s free plan is usually enough. The important practical points are:

- Free for personal use
- Core features included: pages, databases, boards, calendars, basic templates
- Mobile and web apps
- Basic file uploads
- Sufficient for a single project of this size

You likely won’t need the paid plan unless you:

- need advanced permissions
- use large shared workspaces
- need bigger file uploads
- need more version history
- collaborate heavily with a team

For a 3-month solo project, the free tier should be fine unless you’re working with unusually large media files or many collaborators.

---

## 8. It can reduce tool sprawl

One practical advantage of Notion is that it can replace several separate tools:

- Note-taking
- Reference management
- Task management
- Project planning
- Document drafting
- Media organization
- Meeting notes
- Reading list management

That can be useful if you want a single system. Especially for a time-bound project, having fewer tools can mean less context switching.

You can keep:

- your reading list
- your summaries
- your draft
- your tasks
- your sources
- your timeline

all in one place.

If you otherwise use separate tools for notes, tasks, and files, Notion can consolidate that into one project workspace.

---

## 9. It is good for structured drafting

Even though Obsidian is excellent for linked notes, Notion can also be useful for drafting because it supports:

- headings
- checklists
- callouts
- tables
- toggles
- columns
- embedded media
- clear page hierarchy

For a research draft, you can create a page like:

# Draft

## Introduction
- Main argument
- Scope
- Key terms
- Outline of sections

## Literature Review
- Theme 1
- Theme 2
- Gaps identified

## Methodology
- Data sources
- Approach
- Limitations

## Findings
- Pattern 1
- Pattern 2
- Unexpected results

## Discussion
- Interpretation
- Alternative explanations
- Implications

You can use toggles to hide detailed notes while drafting, which can be helpful when writing. You can also keep source links close to the relevant section.

That makes it useful as both a research notebook and a writing workspace.

---

## 10. Notion is stronger if you want “database-ish” organization

If your project will benefit from structured fields, filtering, sorting, and status tracking, Notion has an advantage over plain markdown note-taking.

Examples:

- Which sources are still unfinished?
- Which notes need sources?
- Which sections of the draft are missing evidence?
- Which papers are central vs. background?
- Which tasks block the next writing milestone?
- Which sources are relevant to Theme A but not Theme B?

Those are all easier to answer in Notion if your data is stored in a database with consistent properties.

Plain markdown files can do this too, but it usually takes more manual discipline. Notion makes the structure more explicit.

---

## 11. Sync across devices is automatic

If you use the web app and mobile app, Notion handles synchronization for you. You don’t have to worry about manual sync, syncing folders, or resolving file changes.

For a solo project, this is convenient if you work across:

- laptop
- tablet
- phone
- different computers

The system stays current automatically.

This is a practical plus compared to maintaining a local markdown folder and syncing it with something like Dropbox. With Notion, the service itself is the source of truth.

---

## 12. The built-in search is useful in large projects

For a project that will accumulate many pages and sources, Notion’s search can help you jump between:

- source summaries
- notes
- draft sections
- tasks
- quotations
- files

This can be useful when you lose track of where something is. If you build a consistent naming and tagging system, search becomes much stronger.

---

## Practical workspace suggestion

A good Notion setup for your project might look like this:

### 1. Project Home
A dashboard with links to:

- Source Library
- Notes
- Draft
- Tasks
- Timeline
- Research Questions
- Weekly Review

### 2. Source Library Database
Properties:

- Name
- Type
- Citation
- Status
- Relevance
- Topics
- Date Added
- File
- Notes Link
- Summary

Views:

- Table
- Board by status
- Calendar
- Gallery

### 3. Source Pages
Each source database entry can have a linked page with:

- Full citation
- Summary
- Core claims
- Evidence
- Limitations
- Quotes
- Relevance to project
- Related sources
- Related draft sections

### 4. Notes Database
Properties:

- Title
- Type: idea, observation, argument, question, gap
- Related sources
- Status
- Tags
- Linked draft section

### 5. Draft Page
A central document with:

- Thesis
- Section outline
- Work-in-progress text
- Embedded links to sources and notes
- Revision log

### 6. Task Database
Properties:

- Task
- Status
- Due date
- Priority
- Related source
- Related draft section

### 7. Timeline
A calendar or timeline for:

- reading milestones
- draft deadlines
- revision dates
- submission date

### 8. Weekly Review Page
- What I completed
- What I learned
- What is blocked
- Next week’s focus

---

## Realistic workflow

Here is how you might actually use Notion day to day:

### Morning
Open the Project Home dashboard. Check:

- Tasks due
- Current deadline
- Sources marked as “integrate”
- Draft section currently in progress

### During reading
1. Find or create a source in the Source Library.
2. Attach the PDF or link.
3. Fill in citation and metadata.
4. Write a short summary.
5. Add key quotes.
6. Link the source to relevant notes or draft sections.

### During note-taking
Create notes linked to sources. Use a consistent template so each note answers:

- What is the main idea?
- Why does it matter?
- How does it connect to my project?
- What evidence does it provide?
- What questions does it raise?

### During writing
Work in the Draft page. Link sources directly into sections. Keep a “needs evidence” checklist for each section.

### End of week
Do a weekly review:

- Update source statuses.
- Move tasks.
- Check which sections need more support.
- Look for gaps.
- Plan next week.

That kind of routine can keep the project moving.

---

## Where Notion is especially practical for your case

Given that your project is:

- solo
- 3 months long
- research-based
- includes notes, sources, and drafts
- requires organization
- likely has multiple stages

Notion’s strongest practical advantages are:

1. **Databases for sources and tasks**
2. **Templates for consistency**
3. **Multiple views of the same information**
4. **All-in-one workspace**
5. **Built-in project tracking**
6. **Free personal plan**
7. **Cross-device sync**
8. **Good for both note-taking and drafting**

If you want your system to feel less like “a folder of markdown files” and more like “a managed project environment,” Notion is the better fit.

---

## A few practical mitigations for the known limitations

Since you’ve mentioned spotty Wi-Fi and future portability, there are a few practical ways to reduce the friction of choosing Notion:

### For offline work
- Open your key pages before losing connection.
- Keep a local copy of your current draft in a local word processor or plain text file as a backup while actively writing.
- Use Notion mainly for structuring and organizing, and use a local draft document for heavy writing sessions if needed.

### For portability
- Do a periodic export, even if only at the end of the project.
- Keep an export schedule, for example once a week or at each major milestone.
- If you use lots of custom properties or complex database views, note that their usefulness depends somewhat on staying inside Notion. The text content is more portable than the database structure.

### For performance
- Keep the project workspace focused.
- Use databases for structured items, but don’t turn everything into a massive single database if unnecessary.
- Archive finished source notes and completed drafts.
- Avoid loading very large amounts of media into a single page unless needed.

---

## Bottom line

The practical argument for Notion is that it gives you a **structured, project-based system** rather than just a folder of notes. For a 3-month research project, that structure can save you time in source tracking, planning, drafting, and revision. Its best features for you are likely:

- source databases
- task databases
- templates
- multiple views
- integrated drafting
- cross-device sync
- a single centralized workspace

If you want your research project to feel organized like a small knowledge system or project management environment, Notion is a strong practical choice.

Bottom line: **if you care a lot about iMessage, AirDrop, Handoff, Mac/iPad integration, and resale, I’d pick the iPhone 16. If camera play, customization, a smoother screen, and a lower upfront price matter more—and you don’t really need the Apple ecosystem—I’d pick the Pixel 9.**

For you, specifically: since you already have a Mac and iPad, **my default pick is iPhone 16**, unless you realize that iMessage/Apple continuity isn’t as important to you as you think.

Here’s the break-down.

| Factor | iPhone 16 | Pixel 9 |

## Why I’d lean iPhone 16 for you

Your existing Apple devices change the game.

With iPhone 16 + Mac + iPad, you get:

- AirDrop between devices
- Handoff / copy-paste across devices
- Universal Clipboard
- Continuity camera
- Seamless login / Apple ecosystem handoff
- iMessage / FaceTime within Apple’s bubble
- Easier backup/restore to iCloud
- Usually better resale value

If a meaningful chunk of your friends/family uses iPhone, iMessage is a big deal. You don’t just lose “features”; you lose convenience in group chats, location sharing, read receipts, etc. WhatsApp works fine, but if your social circle lives in iMessage, switching will create friction.

Also, **resale value matters**. A $100 difference at purchase is not as big as it looks once you factor 2–3 years of ownership. iPhone 16 will probably be worth more when you upgrade than Pixel 9.

So if you keep your phone for around 2–3 years, the “real” cost of owning each might end up nearly the same.

## One important correction: Apple is not a B-Corp

I want to gently flag this, because it may be influencing your decision.

To my knowledge, **Apple is not a certified B-Corp**. The phone company most associated with B-Corp certification is **Fairphone**.

That doesn’t mean Apple is unconditionally bad on labor/supply chain. Apple has supplier codes, audits, and supply chain responsibility programs, but it is also a huge company with major supplier issues that have been scrutinized for years. Google also has supplier responsibility audits and reporting.

So if your concern is specifically **“Is the company a certified B-Corp with strong supply chain accountability?”**, neither iPhone 16 nor Pixel 9 clearly satisfies that. In that case, you might look at **Fairphone** as an alternative.

But if you mean “I want a major brand with decent supply chain accountability and not just the cheapest labor,” both Apple and Google are in that space, with mixed records.

## When Pixel 9 is the better choice

I’d pick Pixel 9 if:

1. **You don’t really rely on iMessage**
   If most of your communication is WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, email, or SMS, Pixel loses much of its main downside.

2. **You want a smoother display**
   This is a real daily difference. iPhone 16 has a 6.1″ screen, but it’s **60Hz**. Pixel 9 has a **120Hz display** and a larger 6.3″ screen. If your current phone is old, the Pixel will feel noticeably smoother.

3. **Camera is your #1 priority**
   Pixel 9’s computational photography is excellent, especially for:
   - Low light
   - Night mode
   - Portrait snapshots
   - Magic Eraser
   - Best Take
   - Quick automatic enhancements
   If you just want your phone to make great photos with minimal effort, Pixel is hard to beat.

   iPhone 16’s camera is also very good, especially for:
   - Well-lit photos
   - Social media aesthetics
   - Video
   - 48MP photos
   - Simplicity
   But Pixel’s creative tools are more “fun.”

4. **You want more control**
   Pixel is much more open. You can change launchers, default apps, media libraries, file management, etc. If you like a more Android-flavored experience, that matters.

5. **You want the lower upfront price**
   At $699, Pixel 9 is cheaper. But remember that it will likely be worth less if you sell it later.

## My final recommendation

Given what you described:

- Existing Mac + iPad
- Mentioned iMessage and AirDrop
- Cared about resale
- Already in Apple ecosystem

**I’d go iPhone 16.**

It’s the safer, more integrated upgrade for your current setup, and the better resale value will soften the higher price over time.

But I’d make an exception and choose Pixel 9 if:

- You realize you barely use iMessage
- You don’t care about Apple continuity
- You often send photos to people outside your Apple circle
- You value camera customization
- You want a smoother, larger screen
- You want to spend less upfront

If you’re on the fence, do this quick test:

1. Open iMessage on your current phone.
   - Do you constantly use group iMessage chats?
   - Do you care about FaceTime AirDrop/Handoff with your Mac/iPad?
   - Would your life be annoying without Apple continuity?

If yes → **iPhone 16**.

2. Now think about your camera use.
   - Do you take many low-light photos?
   - Do you want Magic Eraser and quick creative tools?
   - Do you like tinkering with your phone more than keeping it simple?

If yes → **Pixel 9**.

One last money note: check local promotions before deciding. Pixel often gets carrier discounts, trade-in boosts, or seasonal deals. iPhone 16 may be less discounted, but a trade-in deal or refurbished Apple option can change the math.

# Practical Breakdown: iPhone 16

## Ecosystem Integration
For users invested in the Apple ecosystem, the iPhone 16 offers seamless synergy with Mac and iPad devices. Key integrations include:

- **iMessage/Continuity**: Phone calls, SMS, and FaceTime are fully synced across devices, letting you finish a call on your Mac or send texts from your iPad.
- **AirDrop & Handoff**: Instantly share photos, files, and documents between devices without cloud uploads. Start an email on iPhone and continue drafting on Mac.
- **Universal Clipboard & Paste**: Copy text or images once and paste across devices.
- **Shared Features**: iCloud integrates Health, Notes, Calendar, and Files, keeping your personal data consistent. Cross-device search for contacts, photos, or documents is unified.

If your workflow lives in Apple devices, this native interoperability reduces friction in daily tasks—no need for third-party sync apps or manual workarounds.

## Camera & Social Media Utility
The iPhone 16 is optimized for content creation, particularly for social platforms:

- **48 MP Main Sensor + 12 MP Front**: Captures detailed 12MP grid-compatible images (ideal for Instagram grid displays) and wide-angle shots.
- **4K 120fps Video**: Smooth slow-motion content with shallow depth-of-field (f/1.8). Action stabilization keeps handheld clips steady.
- **Portrait Mode with Real-Time Light Adjustments**: Auto-applies studio-like lighting. Easy editing post-shot.
- **Macro Mode**: Close-up photography for detail-oriented content.
- **Quick Edits/Social Templates**: Built-in filters and crosspost tools for direct sharing to Instagram, TikTok, and X (Twitter) within the native camera app.

For frequent social media creators, the balance of image quality, video performance, and streamlined sharing workflow makes it a strong choice.

## Price & Long-Term Value
The $799 price point includes:

- **Higher Resale Value**: iPhones (especially base models) retain 40–60% of value after 2 years, reducing total cost of ownership if you upgrade every 2–3 years.
- **5+ Years of OS Updates**: Apple typically supports new iPhone models with major iOS updates for 5 years, with security patches beyond that. Longevity accounts for the upfront premium.
- **Year 2 Tax Exemption**: (If applicable in some regions, e.g., UK VAT-free trade-in offers at Apple Store or authorized resellers until Sept 30, 2025, potentially dropping net cost to $699.)
- **CarPlay & Enterprise MDM Compatibility**: If your work or Mac/iPad is under university/corporate Apple MDM, the iPhone auto-enrolls. This saves IT integration time.

## Practical Limitations
- **Limited Customization**: No third-party launchers, limited widget customization, and no full app sideloading (though limited iOS 17.4+ developer sideloading exists for non-MDOf developers). If you require launchers, multiple magnifiers, or custom UI layouts, Android (Pixel) is more flexible.
- **No charger in Box**: You'll need a USB-C to Lightning adapter (if not switching to USB-C) or a MagSafe charger for fast wireless charging.
- **Trade-off Ecosystem Lock-in**: If you plan to keep using non-Apple tablets/desktops long-term, the lock-in is a consideration. But if your devices are Mac/iPad, this skill is a net positive.

## Final Verdict
Given your stated ecosystem (Mac/iPad), social media focus, and long-term value considerations, the iPhone 16 offers:

- Superior cross-device convenience (Handoff, AirDrop, iMessage continuity)
- Content creation tailored for social platforms (4K120fps, auto-lighting portrait, instant share tools)
- Strong residual value and multi-year OS support
- Work/school MDM readiness if relevant

The $100 price difference over the Pixel 9 is offset by higher resale value, longer OS support, and seamless ecosystem integration that reduces daily friction. If maximizing customization or pixel-perfect edits matter more than device synergy, Pixel wins. But for a unified Apple workflow and social-first content creation, the iPhone 16 is the practical choice.

Here's how I'd think about it:

## The hybrid approach wins here

Your best move is actually **both** — use the SSD for the initial fast, private backup, then also upload an **encrypted** copy to Google Drive. Here's why:

1. **Security first**: You're right to be concerned about Google's US jurisdiction and content scanning. The fix is to encrypt the files *before* uploading (VeraCrypt container, 7z AES-256 archive, or a tool like Cryptomator). Google then only sees an unintelligible blob, and nowhere in their ToS/scanning policies can they read your actual documents.

2. **You get all the upsides of both options**:
   - The 30-min SSD backup stays fully private and on-your-side the whole time
   - The encrypted Drive copy means you can actually retrieve files from the repair shop (or anywhere) without physically hauling the SSD around — which solves your accessibility headache
   - If the SSD physically fails or gets lost, the Drive copy is your safety net (and vice versa, if ever the Drive account has issues, the SSD is still intact)

3. **It kills the single-point-of-failure problem**: Right now both options have a failure mode. Drive = jurisdiction/scan risk. SSD = physical risk. Having two independent copies at different locations is standard practice for sensitive data.

4. **On the Shenzhen aside**: If the SSD is from a reputable brand (Samsung, WD, SanDisk, Kingston, etc.) with decent key specs, the "made in Shenzhen" thing isn't a real reliability concern — most well-known drives are made there. If it's a no-name or suspiciously cheap brand, consider swapping it for a quality one *before* trusting it with client data — for 50GB, a decent 500GB external is cheap insurance. While you're at it, copy the files over, then verify (spot-check a few documents, or run a checksum like sha256sum against a list to make sure nothing is truncated/corrupt).

## Practical steps for tonight

1. Back up to the SSD (30 min), plug it in, verify a few files open properly.
2. Create an encrypted container/archive containing all 50GB.
3. Upload that encrypted blob to Google Drive (run in the background, 2 hours or so).
4. Store the passphrase/key somewhere separate from *both* devices — your password manager on your phone is ideal, just make sure the phone isn't the thing going into repair.
5. Optional but recommended: test-decrypt a sample file on a different device (phone → Drive app is clunky but doable, or borrow a laptop) to confirm the whole chain actually works. Don't skip this — an untested backup tonight is a panic tomorrow.

If for any reason you can only do one: with truly sensitive client documents, I'd still lean toward the encrypted Drive copy as the *primary* (remote access + redundancy), with the SSD as secondary. The one scenario that really hurts is needing those files mid-repair and not having the SSD on you. If compliance matters to you (legal/medical client data), check whether your client agreements or bar/medical board rules even *allow* cloud storage — encryption layers usually satisfy most of those policies, but worth knowing.

That's the move: encrypt, go both, verify before you sleep.

# Why Venmo Makes Sense (Practically Speaking)

- **Upfront cost**: Both options come in at $0 for standard transfers, so price isn’t a deciding factor—either way you’re not paying a fee to send the $500.

- **Speed for friend**: If your friend also uses Venmo, the $500 lands in their Venmo balance the moment you hit send, and they’ll get an immediate notification. Even if they want to move it to a bank later, standard bank transfers are about 1–3 business days, which is still a known, predictable window you can mention ahead of time.

- **Friction of sending**: You described the Venmo flow as one tap and done—this is a real convenience win. You don’t have to double-check a bank name or confirm a linked Zelle email, you just pick the contact in your app.

- **Privacy control**: Since the feed is your main concern, you can set the payment private before you send it and it stays out of the social feed. That single extra tap neutralizes the privacy downside without losing the convenience benefits.

- **App integration & context**: Because the payment is tied to a group trip you’re both already tracking, Venmo lets you send it from chat, tag a shared event, or make it part of a longer transaction history (like a bill split) if other items come up later. That ambient context makes it less likely either of you has to reference a separate message thread to remember what it was for.

- **Comparison to Zelle path**: Zelle is good when you *need* money to move bank-to-bank in an instant, but here your friend doesn’t necessarily need the cash in a checking account by tonight—they just need it paid to you. Venmo covers the “you owe me” part efficiently and keeps the record in a place both of you already check anyway.

In short: pick Venmo when you value the instant, in-app one-tap flow, the message context around group expenses, and the option to keep it private—because none of Zelle’s bank-to-bank speed is needed for this particular payment.

- You value **getting seen quickly**. A same-week slot is a real advantage when you have a new problem or something that can’t wait three weeks.
- You want **multiply quick follow-up** via portal. That’s a big deal in primary care, because a lot of care happens during message follow-ups, medication adjustments, review of abnormal labs, etc.

## I’d lean toward **Dr. Patel** if…
- You strongly prefer **longer, thorough appointments**, and you sometimes get frustrated when visits feel rushed.
- You have **multiple chronic conditions**, complex labs, or issues that benefit from in-depth visits.

- Addressed your actual concerns, not just a checklist

## Why Obsidian fits a research project well

### 1. Plain markdown files are future-proof
If your project produces a paper, report, proposal, or long document, having everything as plain `.md` files is a big advantage.

You can:

- Move the vault to another machine easily.
- Copy it to an external drive.
- Use Git for version control if you want.
- Open the notes in many other tools later.
- Avoid relying on one vendor’s export format.

With Notion, export is possible, but as you noted, some structure can get flattened or lost, especially for complex databases.

### 2. Linking works naturally for research
Obsidian’s linking model is very good for researching because you can make:

- One note per source.
- One note per concept.
- One note per argument.
- One note per draft section.
- One note per interview, article, dataset, or idea.

For example, a source note can look like this:

```markdown
---
type: source
title: "Example Study on Something"
authors: Smith, Johnson
year: 2023
url: https://example.com
tags: [source, article]
status: summarized
---

Why this matters to the project:
- Shows relationship between X and Y.

Key claims:
- Claim 1...
- Claim 2...

Quotes:
> "..."

Connections:
- Supports: [[Claim about X]]
- Contradicts: [[Earlier idea on Y]]
- Useful for: [[Draft section 2]]
```

```markdown
Definition:
...

Evidence:
- [[Smith 2023]] argues that X increases Y.
- [[Jones 2021]] suggests the effect is context-dependent.

Open questions:
- Does this hold when Z changes?
- What is the mechanism?
```

Over time, this creates a web of evidence without forcing everything into rigid table rows.

### 3. It handles notes, sources, and drafts without over-structuring
A good simple structure could be:

```text
Research Project/
  00_Project Overview/
  10_Sources/
  20_Concepts/
  30_Drafts/
  40_Tasks and Meta/
  90_Templates/
  Attachments/
```

You can keep it even simpler. Sometimes a flat structure with good tags and links is better than deep folders.

For example:

```text
Vault/
  Sources/
  Notes/
  Drafts/
  Templates/
  Attachments/
```

That may be enough for three months.

### 4. The sync cost is manageable if you’re solo
Obsidian itself is free. The paid Sync service is convenient, but you do not have to use it. You can use:

- iCloud
- Dropbox
- OneDrive
- Syncthing
- Git

This works, but it is slightly less polished than Notion’s built-in cloud experience. If you are mostly on one or two devices, it is usually not a problem.

### 5. Plugins can be powerful, but you don’t need many
You do not need to get lost in Obsidian’s plugin ecosystem.

For a research project, a minimal starting set might be:

- Core templates
- Backlinks
- Tags
- Search
- Excalidraw or Canvas, only if you want whiteboard-style thinking
- Dataview, only if you want simple database-like queries inside markdown
- Zotero-related plugins, only if you use Zotero

If you start with too many plugins, the system can become work. A simple vault with source notes, concept notes, links, tags, and a few templates will likely be enough.

## When Notion is the better choice

Notion is a great tool, and it may be the better choice for you if your project needs more of the following:

### 1. Strong database views
If you mostly need to manage sources as rows in a table, Notion can be immediately useful.

For example:

| Source | Type | Author | Year | Topic | Status | Key takeaway | Link to draft |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Smith 2023 | Article | Smith | 2023 | X | Summarized | Supports hypothesis A | [[Intro draft]] |
| Jones 2021 | Book chapter | Jones | 2021 | Y | Skimmed | Complicates argument B | [[Section 2]] |

Notion is excellent if you want table views, kanban boards, calendars, and filters.

If your main organizing problem is “I have 80 sources and I need to track their status, category, author, year, and contribution to the paper,” Notion may feel more immediately structured.

### 2. Collaboration
If your research project involves group members, supervisors, classmates, or collaborators who need access to the same notes, Notion is easier.

Obsidian can share notes, but it is not built around real-time collaborative editing and shared workspaces in the same way.

### 3. You want a polished cloud experience
Notion works well as a cloud first app. If you want seamless access across devices without setting up local file sync, Notion is smoother.

### 4. You prefer visual organization over file-based organization
Some people prefer a spatial, shared workspace where pages are cards, databases, boards, and subpages. If that suits you, Notion may feel better.

## The main tradeoff

The core difference is this:

- **Notion** is better when the structure of your project is external: databases, statuses, assignments, shared pages, filters, table views.
- **Obsidian** is better when the heart of your project is thinking, connecting ideas, sources, and writing.

For a research project involving **notes, sources, and drafts**, the latter often matters more.

## My recommended approach

I would suggest choosing **Obsidian** and using a deliberately simple workflow.

### Week 1 setup

Create a vault with basic folders:

```text
Sources/
Concepts/
Drafts/
Templates/
Attachments/
Project/
```

Create three templates.

### Source template

```markdown
title:
authors:
year:
url:
doi:

---

## Key claims

## Quotes

## How it connects to my project

## Links

- Related concepts:
- Related sources:
- Draft sections:
```

### Concept template

```markdown

tags:
status:
---

## Definition

## Why it matters

## Evidence

## Counterarguments / complications

## Open questions

## Related notes
```

### Draft template

```markdown

type: draft
section:
status:
tags:
---

## Purpose of this section

## Main argument

## Evidence needed

## Sources

## Draft text

## Notes to self
```

### Basic workflow

1. **Read a source?**
   - Create a source note.
   - Summarize the main claim.
   - Extract important quotes.
   - Link it to relevant concept notes.

2. **Develop an idea?**
   - Create a concept note.
   - Link to sources that support, complicate, or contradict it.

3. **Write a draft?**
   - Create a draft note by section.
   - Link the relevant concept and source notes.
   - Write around the links.

4. **Review weekly?**
   - Ask:
     - What do I understand less clearly now?
     - Which sources need deeper reading?
     - Which sections are undersupported?
     - Which notes are disconnected and should be linked?

This keeps the system from becoming a catalog where notes are filed but never used.

## A practical recommendation

Given what you described, I’d choose **Obsidian** because:

- The project is three months, long enough for structure to matter but short enough that you may not want to over-invest in Notion setup.
- You explicitly value portable markdown exports.
- You are organizing notes, sources, and drafts, which is a natural fit for linked markdown notes.
- You can manage sync with another option.
- You do not seem to prioritize real-time collaboration.
- You can start simple and add plugins only if needed.

## When I would switch my recommendation to Notion

I would recommend **Notion** instead if any of these apply strongly:

- You need to manage many sources with lots of metadata and want instant table/kanban views.
- You will be collaborating closely with other people in the project.
- You want a polished cloud workspace with less file-sync setup.
- You would rather build the project structure upfront than evolve it through notes.
- You are less interested in long-term portability and more interested in immediate organization and accessibility.

## Bottom line

For a solo, three-month research project focused on **notes, sources, and drafts**, I’d probably start with **Obsidian**. Keep it lean: source notes, concept notes, draft notes, links, tags, and a few templates. Use the plain markdown files as a backup and export safety net.

If, after a week or two, you find that you constantly need table views, status tracking, or collaboration, then Notion may be the better fit. But for research thinking and writing, Obsidian feels like the safer and more durable choice.

response:
Short answer: **for a three-month, mostly solo research project, I’d probably start with Obsidian**, unless you specifically need a shared workspace or a polished database of sources. Your main criteria should be: *what can you set up quickly, actually use every day for three months, and still have something usable afterward?* On that test, Obsidian usually wins for individual research notes and drafts.

## My pick: Obsidian, with a simple setup

Obsidian makes more sense if:

- You’re mostly working solo.
- You want to jot notes, quote sources, write drafts, and link ideas without configuring a bunch of databases.
- You care about owning your files in plain Markdown.
- You want low-friction note-taking and fast local file access.
- You may want to keep some notes after the project ends.
- You already have a way to sync/backup via Dropbox, iCloud, OneDrive, Git, etc.

For a three-month project, you do not want to spend a week becoming a systems architect. You want a folder structure and a template that help you get things out of your head quickly.

One small caveat: I’m not able to verify the claim about Obsidian and industrial-fishing lobbying. If that is something you care a lot about, check it out separately. But for a three-month project, I would not let an unconfirmed business-ethics concern outweigh the basic practical tradeoffs unless you are strongly opposed to the company.

## When Notion makes more sense

Notion is a better choice if:

- You are working with a team, advisor, collaborators, or want easy sharing.
- You need structured source tracking: status, type, journal, DOI, tags, dates, linked notes, etc.
- You like database views, filters, and maybe a timeline or kanban board.
- You want the easiest built-in sync across devices without configuring a third-party sync solution.
- You mostly think in “pages and databases” rather than folders and files.

Notion’s strength is that a source can be a row in a database:

```
Title | Authors | Year | Type | Status | Citation | Key claims | Linked notes
```

That is genuinely useful for research. If your main problem is tracking lots of papers/articles/books and their processing status, Notion may be worth the setup time.

But its downside is that it is more locked in. You can export to Markdown, as you said, but some formatting and database structure can be lost or flattened. For a three-month project, that may not matter. For a long-term personal knowledge base, it matters more.

## The core tradeoff

| Factor | Obsidian | Notion |
|---|---:|---:|
| Setup time | Usually lower if you keep it simple | Can take longer if you overconfigure |
| File ownership | Best — plain Markdown files | Worse — app/database dependent |
| Source database | Good with templates/frontmatter/plugins | Strong out of the box |
| Drafting notes | Very good | Very good |
| Collaboration | Weak/limited | Strong |
| Offline/local use | Excellent | Good, but less native to its model |
| Sync | Needs Dropbox/iCloud/Git/etc. | Built-in sync |
| Long-term portability | Excellent | Good, but export may lose structure |

For a three-month solo research project, I’d weight **setup cost** and **file portability** heavily. Obsidian is usually the safer minimal system.

## Don’t overbuild it

The biggest mistake with either tool is spending more time organizing the system than doing the research. For three months, the ideal system should take no more than an hour to set up and should not require much maintenance.

A good rule:

> Choose the tool where adding your first 10 sources, 10 notes, and 2 draft sections feels almost effortless.

If Obsidian feels too manual after a few days, switch to Notion. Migrating from Obsidian to Notion is easier than the reverse, because Obsidian notes are just files.

## If you choose Obsidian: keep it boring and usable

Do not start by installing 30 plugins. You probably need very few for three months.

A simple vault structure:

```
/00 Inbox
/10 Sources
/20 Notes
/30 Drafts
/90 Templates
/attachments
```

Then use a source template like this:

```markdown
---
type: article
title: 
authors: 
year: 
source: 
doi: 
status: unread
tags: [topic]
---

## First impression

## Key claims

## Quotes

## My assessment

## Links
```

Use filenames that work without clicking into the file:

```
2025-01-15_Smith_2020_UrbanHeatIslands.md
```

or:

```
2024-03-11_Interview_Maria_Minnoworks.md
```

That matters after three months when you’re searching for something and only remember fragments.

For syncing/backups, pick one:

- Dropbox folder
- iCloud folder
- OneDrive folder
- Git repo, if you are comfortable
- Local backup + occasional archive

Test the backup. The system is only as good as your ability to restore it.

I would also avoid getting obsessed with the graph view. It is fun, but for a three-month project it may be more distraction than utility. The graph becomes more helpful when notes are densely linked and the project is long enough that the structure interests you.

## If you choose Notion: make it lean

If you go Notion, I would not try to build a full personal knowledge system. I would make one project page with:

- `/Sources`
- `/Notes`
- `/Drafts`
- `/Meetings`
- `/Decisions`

Then create one source database with simple properties:

```
Title
Type: article / book / interview / dataset / other
Status: unread / reading / summarized / synthesized
Date added
Citation
Summary
Linked notes
```

That may be enough. Avoid adding too many relations, rollups, dashboards, and views until you actually need them.

I would also export your workspace weekly or biweekly, not just at the end. For a three-month project, a lightweight export habit reduces lock-in risk and gives you a safety net.

## Hybrid option

If you are torn, a hybrid can work, but it adds overhead:

- Use **Obsidian** for notes, quotes, drafts, and thinking.
- Use **Notion** just as a lightweight source database/tracker.

This can be nice if your notes are becoming long and messy, but you still want a structured table of sources. For example:

- Reading list and status: Notion.
- Analytical notes: Obsidian.
- Drafts: Obsidian.
- Shared project page or source list: Notion.

But for a three-month project, I would only do this if the source tracking problem is really the bottleneck. Otherwise, one system is simpler.

## My practical recommendation

If I had to choose for you, I would say:

1. **Start with Obsidian** if you are solo, writing-heavy, and want a portable low-friction system.
2. **Choose Notion** if you need collaboration, a polished source database, or built-in sync with minimal third-party setup.
3. **Do not spend more than one setup session on either one.**
4. **After one week, ask yourself: “Am I actually using this daily, or am I just organizing it?”**
5. If Obsidian feels too manual, move your Markdown files into Notion.

For your situation, assuming you are mostly working alone and want notes, sources, and drafts in one place, **Obsidian is probably the better default for a three-month project**. Just keep the setup simple: folders, one template, and a backup.

For **focused work a few days a week**, I’d lean toward **The Hive** *if you’re comfortable with a 3-month commitment*. But **WeWork is the safer choice if flexibility, variety, or phone booths matter a lot to you**.

Here’s the breakdown:

### Where The Hive looks stronger
- **Lower cost:** $200 vs. $350 is a **$150/month difference**. If you go 3 days a week, that’s **$50/day** extra with WeWork.
- **Shorter, lower-friction commute:** A 12-minute walk is easier to sustain than a 15-minute drive/radius, especially if the weather is bad or you’re rushing.
- **Smaller community:** If your goal is concentration plus some human connection, 30 members and weekly lunches can feel less overwhelming than a large coworking scene.
- **Probably quieter / more residential-goalkan:** Smaller local spots often feel less “hubby” and more conducive to focus, though that depends on the actual layout and time of day.

### Where WeWork looks stronger
- **Month-to-month:** You can try it for a month without being locked in.
- **Three nearby locations:** This is a real perk if you want variety or if one space is too crowded.
- **Phone booths:** If you take calls a lot, this is a meaningful advantage.
- **More amenities and structure:** Event space, broader community, likely more professional setup overall.
- **Sustainability angle:** If carbon negative/reforestation matters to you, that’s an extra point in WeWork’s favor.

### The biggest decision factor
For your stated purpose — **escaping home and getting some focused work in a few days a week** — I’d rank:

1. **Quiet/ability to focus**
2. **Ease of getting there**
3. **Cost per day actually used**
4. **Community**
5. **Extras**

On that list, **The Hive probably wins** if the 3-month minimum is not a dealbreaker. At 12 minutes away and $150 cheaper, it’s the better value for regular, repeated use.

### I’d choose The Hive if:
- You think you’ll use it consistently for at least a quarter
- You don’t need multiple locations
- You don’t depend heavily on phone booths
- You like the idea of a smaller, warmer community

### I’d choose WeWork if:
- You want to test the waters with only a 1-month commitment
- You like having multiple nearby options
- You need private spaces for calls
- You care more about amenities/community scale than minimizing cost

### My actual recommendation
If I were you, I’d **visit both in person at the time you’d likely work** and check:
- noise level
- desk density
- Wi‑fi
- coffee/barrel
- how easy it is to get a phone booth or meeting room
- how comfortable you feel commuting there

Then I’d do this:
- **Try WeWork for one month** if you want low risk
- **Switch to The Hive for 3 months** if you decide it’s the better fit after that

That gives you a cheap “pilot” period with WeWork before committing to The Hive.

### Bottom line
- **Better value for focused work a few days a week:** **The Hive**
- **Better flexibility and amenities:** **WeWork**
- **Most practical choice to start:** **Try WeWork for a month, then move to The Hive if it fits** — unless the 3-month lock-in makes you nervous, in which case WeWork is the smarter default.

response:
# Why Linear Makes Sense for Our Team

Given that both tools cost the same—$8/user/month, or $64 total for our team of eight—the decision should come down to how well each tool fits our actual daily work, not price. On that front, Linear is the cleaner, more practical fit for us right now.

## Faster Day-to-Day Workflow
Jira is powerful, but that flexibility comes with overhead. Configuring boards, managing custom fields, and working through layered workflows can make even simple actions feel heavy. Linear is more focused: cycles, projects, and issues flow naturally without a lot of setup. For our team, that means less time spent wrestling with the tool and more time actually doing the engineering work. It’s faster to create an issue, move work forward, and get visibility into status.

## Easier Learning Curve
Most of us have seen Jira before, which is a point in its favor. But “familiar” doesn’t necessarily mean “fast to use effectively.” Jira’s complexity means there’s still a real learning curve for using it well. Linear is intentionally more opinionated, which makes it easier to pick up and comfortable in daily use from the start. For a small team that wants momentum, that’s a meaningful advantage.

## Modern Integrations
Linear’s GitHub integration fits neatly into how we build and ship code. Commit references, pull requests, and issue tracking connect in a way that keeps context right where the work is happening. While Jira has integrations too, Linear’s approach feels tighter and less disrupted by context-switching.

## Right Size for the Team
Jira shines when you need to model complex, multi-team workflows at scale. We don’t. We’re a small engineering team, and our processes are straightforward enough that Linear’s built-in structure works out of the box. We wouldn’t need to spend time customizing to force it to behave the way we want—it already does.

## Bottom Line
Since both tools are the same price, choosing the one that reduces friction makes the most sense. Linear gives us a fast, focused, and low-maintenance way to manage work, with integrations that fit how we build. It keeps us unblocked, keeps the process simple, and lets us invest our energy into shipping rather than adapting to the tool.

I’d go with the **external SSD**, but — and this is the big one — **only if you also remove those files from the laptop before it leaves your hands.**

Here’s the paranoid-logician version of why:

* Your laptop is going to a repair shop, which means a stranger will have physical access to your storage. If the sensitive client documents are still on the internal drive, backing them up elsewhere doesn’t actually *secure* them — it just makes a second copy while the original stays in someone else’s hands.
* For genuinely sensitive client material, your Google Drive option has a real wrinkle beyond “they can scan it”: most client agreements (NDA, confidentiality, data-handling) will implicitly or explicitly expect you to control where the data lives. Stepping across into a US-jurisdiction cloud for client documents without checking the contract is a way to have a very awkward conversation later, especially if anything goes wrong there.
* The 30-min USB 3.0 copy is the fastest, most deterministic option — no upload bandwidth variance, no 2-hour “praying the connection doesn’t drop” window.

To make the SSD route as solid as you can on short notice:

1. Copy the 50 GB.
2. Verify it (spot-check a sample of files, ideally run a checksum pass or at least confirm file counts/sizes match).
3. Encrypt the drive if you can (BitLocker / FileVault / VeraCrypt). If the drive is lost or stolen overnight, this makes the data actually private, not just “in your pocket.”
4. After verifying the backup, securely delete the original client documents from the laptop before it ships off. If you’re on BitLocker/FileVault and can’t fully re-provision the drive, at minimum delete the specific sensitive directories and confirm they’re gone.
5. Keep the SSD with you at home, not at the repair shop.

If client contracts specifically require cloud redundancy or you’re in a situation where you truly can’t risk a single-copy failure, then *after* the SSD copy you can also push to Google Drive as a second layer and, if you want maximum paranoia, delete the cloud copy after a day or two. But the SSD-first approach is the right call for this situation.

response:
The short version: **for a single W‑2 plus ~$15k of straightforward freelance consulting, TurboTax Self-Employed is probably the better value if things are simple.** But if you want expert backup, annual planning, more peace of mind, or there are any “messy” items involved, the $350 CPA is definitely defensible.

A few important caveats: I’m not a CPA/tax pro here, and the right answer depends on your state, filing status, total income, exact freelance structure, and what kinds of business expenses you have. But based on what you described, here’s how I’d weigh it.

# Where TurboTax Self-Employed makes the most sense

TurboTax is a very reasonable option if your freelance situation is basically:

- **Independent contractor / self-employed as a sole proprietor**
- You received **1099-NEC** income
- You do **not** have employees
- You do **not** have a separate S-corp or complicated entity
- You are **not** generating out-of-state source income
- You have **a manageable list of business expenses**
- Your W‑2 withholding is probably enough to cover the extra tax, or you can figure out estimated payments
- You are comfortable with a guided questionnaire and double-checking your answers

At ~$15k, the freelance piece is not huge enough that you should necessarily pay an extra $230 just to have someone do it, **unless** the CPA is likely to uncover meaningful deductions or you really want that safety net.

Also, if you’ve already been comfortable with basic TurboTax, the jump to Self-Employed is not that huge. The main new piece is the **Schedule C / self-employment tax** part. The software will walk you through:

- Gross consulting income
- Business expenses
- Net profit
- Self-employment tax
- QBI deduction, if applicable
- Interaction with your W‑2 income

It’s not scary. You just need to be careful not to put in overly aggressive or unsupported deductions.

# Where the CPA starts to make more sense

I’d lean more toward the CPA if any of these are true:

1. **You have a lot of business expense categories**
   For example:
   - Home office
   - Vehicle/mileage
   - Meals with clients
   - Travel
   - Software subscriptions
   - Cell phone / internet allocation
   - Contracts / co-worker costs
   - Insurance
   - Training / professional development
   - Gear / equipment

   If your list is long and you don’t want to misclassify things, a CPA may be worth it.

2. **You drive for the business or work from home**
   Those are the two classic places where self-employed filers make mistakes. Mileage and home office rules are common error areas. If your consulting involves real mileage or a dedicated home office, a CPA may save you from mistakes.

3. **You have income or expenses in more than one state**
   That can get complicated, especially if you were a remote worker who lived in one state but had clients or assigned work in another.

4. **You want actual planning, not just data entry**
   A CPA can talk through things like:
   - Adjusting W‑2 withholding
   - Estimated tax payments
   - IRA / HSA / 401(k) choices
   - Business entity structure
   - Reasonable business deductions
   - Next-year planning

   If you only want your return filed, software is fine. If you want a second brain, CPA is better.

5. **You just want someone to answer if something comes up**
   Especially if you get a state notice, a 1099 discrepancy, or something confusing during the year.

6. **The freelance part is not really “just consulting”**
   If it’s more complex than a normal 1099 side income, CPA becomes much more attractive.

# The brokerage piece

This part may be less “brokerage contributions” and more “taxable events.” If you mean you put money into a **regular taxable brokerage account**, that itself is not usually taxable or deductible. What matters are the items that show up on your tax return:

- Interest
- Dividends
- Capital gains
- Capital losses
- 1099-B / 1099-DIV / 1099-INT activity

If you’re just holding a brokerage account and the amounts are normal, neither TurboTax nor a CPA is necessarily required. But a CPA might do a slightly better job if there are:

- Wash sale issues
- Amended cost basis
- Carried-forward losses
- Taxable account sales
- Positive/negative interaction with other income

If it’s only routine interest and dividends, software handles that easily.

# The $230 difference

This is the real practical question.

**TurboTax route:**
- Cost: ~$120
- Maybe add audit support if you want

**CPA route:**
- Cost: $350
- Difference: $230

So the CPA only “pays for itself” if they either:
- Catch a deduction/credit that comfortably exceeds $230
- Avoid an error that would cost you more
- Save you meaningful planning time
- Give you meaningful peace of mind

A good CPA often can find more than $230 in deductions if you have real business expenses. But if your freelance activity is simple and expenses are minimal, the extra $230 might not be worth it.

# The lobbying donation issue

You mentioned the CPA donates part of fees to industrial fishing lobbying. I’d treat that as a separate values decision. For many people, that amounts to only a tiny fraction of the fee and wouldn’t matter. But if it genuinely bothers you, that may be a more important factor than the tax mechanics themselves.

One nuance: if that donation is tied to a provider or network, it might be unavoidable. If it is a direct part of the CPA’s own model and you do not like it, I would factor that seriously.

# My lean, based on your facts

If things are truly **simple W‑2 + $15k consulting + normal brokerage activity**, I’d probably start with **TurboTax Self-Employed**.

Why? Because:

- The freelance amount is not high enough to demand a professional by default
- The software guides you through Schedule C pretty well
- Your main risk is overspending or misclassifying deductions, which you can control
- You save about $200+
- You avoid the values issue around third-party lobbying

But I would choose the **CPA** if:

- You have a lot of mileage or home office use
- You have many business expenses
- You’re unsure whether your income is fully reportable or properly categorized
- You have out-of-state issues
- You want ongoing advice all year
- You strongly prefer “send it, they handle it”

# Questions that would flip my answer

If any of these are yes, the CPA becomes more attractive:

- Did you actually keep records of business expenses?
- Do you have a home office?
- Do you drive for business?
- Did you take business meals?
- Are you incorporated, or do you have any entity-based filings?
- Did you earn compensation in another state?
- Is your W‑2 withholding low?
- Do you expect to have continuing self-employment income for several years?
- Would you pay extra $230 purely for comfort and convenience?

# If you go TurboTax, watch out for these

Since your biggest worry is the freelance part, these are the most common tripwires:

1. **You need to separate business and personal expenses**
   If you use a phone, computer, or car partly for business, you generally need a consistent method. If you’re not doing any business expense allocation, that’s fine. If you are, do it cleanly.

2. **Do not “over” claim deductions to justify the software fee**
   The CPA concern people have is fair, but the bigger practical risk is unsupported deductions. Take only what you can document.

3. **Self-employment tax is real**
   Freelance income can create self-employment tax even if you have a W‑2 too. If your withholding is low, you may want to look at estimated tax payments.

4. **QBI may apply, but don’t hand-wave it**
   You may have a qualified business income deduction tied to the consulting profit, but it interacts with total income and the nature of the business. TurboTax handles it, but the inputs matter.

5. **Brokerage income is about the tax forms, not “contributions”**
   Focus on the actual 1099s and realized gains/losses.

6. **Save the backup**
   Keep invoices, expense logs, mileage logs, business desktops/bank statements, and your 1099s. Audits are uncommon at this income level, but if anything ever comes up, documentation is everything.

# If you go CPA, ask these before committing

Before deciding, it would be worth asking the CPA:

- Does the $350 cover federal plus state?
- Does it include e-filing?
- Does it include self-employment tax analysis?
- Does it include QBI?
- Do you get an email/phone consult if something comes up?
- Do you provide audit support?
- Is the lobbying donation a required part of the fee?
- How long will turnaround be?
- Do you work with first-time Schedule C filers?

That will tell you whether you’re getting real value or just a data-entry service.

# Bottom line

**If this is a normal W‑2 person with $15k of consulting and no major complications, I’d lean TurboTax Self-Employed.**

**If you want confidence, planning, or you have a bunch of business expenses, mileage, home office, multi-state issues, or ongoing self-employment income, the CPA is worth the extra $230.**

If you want, I can also help you make a quick “am I too complicated for software?” call. Just answer a few things:
- Do you have a home office?
- Do you drive for the work?
- Do you have out-of-state client work?
- Do you have more than a few business expense categories?
- Is your income from a sole prop or an LLC/S-corp?

# Notion vs. Obsidian: Practical Comparison for a 3-Month Research Project

## Overview
For a three-month solo research project, the priority is organizing notes, sources, and drafts in a way that supports tracking, quick access, and low overhead. Notion and Obsidian both offer strong features, but they take different approaches. The comparison below focuses on how each tool maps to the practical needs of this project.

## Key Criteria

| Criterion | Notion | Obsidian |
|---|---|---|
| **Note & Source Organization** | Native databases with properties (e.g., status, tags, dates) and linkable relations. Enables structured tracking for literature, notes, and tasks. | Local Markdown files with links and tags. Database-like features require plugins (e.g., Dataview), adding setup. |
| **Templates** | Large library of ready-made templates, including research workflows. Can be customized quickly. | Template system exists, but is more manual. Community templates are available but less polished. |
| **Collaboration & Sharing** | Can share pages via URL with viewer/editor permissions. Supports comments and real-time updates, making advisor or colleague review simple. | Sharing requires exporting to PDF/Markdown/HTML, creating friction for collaborators not using Obsidian. |
| **Cross-Device Sync** | Built-in cloud sync with real-time updates. Works in browser, desktop, and mobile. Offline access to previously viewed pages is available. | Stores files locally, synced via services like Dropbox. Full offline access, but potential for sync conflicts and extra setup. |
| **Performance** | Reliable for moderate-sized workspaces. Performance may slow with very large projects, but unlikely to be an issue for a three-month scope. | Highly performant, even with large vaults. Speed advantage is less critical for a focused, short-term project. |
| **Integrations** | Native integrations with tools like Slack, Google Drive, and task managers, simplifying broader workflow appending. | Extensible via plugins, but fewer native integrations and more manual setup. |
| **Portability** | Content can be exported to Markdown. Some formatting (e.g., databases) may simplify during export. | Local Markdown files are highly portable with no formatting loss. This is a key strength for long-term use. |

## Why Notion Fits This Project

1. **Structured Databases for Research Workflows**
   - Notion's inline databases make it easy to track sources (with properties like author, DOI, and status) and link them directly to notes. This reduces the need to switch between separate files or formats. For example, a sources database can be connected to note pages, making it straightforward to see which papers have been read, summarized, or cited.
   - Obsidian can achieve similar functionality with plugins, but this introduces extra configuration time and complexity. For a project with a defined timeline, Notion's out-of-the-box database features offer a more immediate and visually clean workflow.

2. **Templates Accelerate Setup**
   - Notion's template library includes research-oriented templates (e.g., literature reviews, note structures, or project dashboards). This reduces initial setup time, allowing a focus on content creation rather than customizing a blank system. While Obsidian's templates are useful, they are more basic and may require more manual effort to adapt for complex research needs.

3. **Simplified Collaboration for Progress Sharing**
   - Sharing work with an advisor or colleagues is a practical consideration, particularly when seeking feedback. Notion's URL-based permissions make it easy to provide read-only or editable access to specific pages. This contrasts with Obsidian, where exportation in separate formats is required for sharing, potentially leading to versioning issues or formatting disruptions. For regular check-ins, Notion's integrated review process is less friction-heavy.

4. **Sync and Accessibility Without Extra Infrastructure**
   - Notion's built-in cloud sync means there's no reliance on third-party services like Dropbox, eliminating potential sync conflicts or setup hurdles. While offline access is more limited than Obsidian's local file model, a three-month project that primarily uses reliable internet connections (e.g., at a research site or in controlled environments) can mitigate this. Even with lower connectivity, Notion's offline view of previously opened pages allows for review, reducing the risk of interruptions.

5. **Project Scope Aligns with Notion's Strengths**
   - Obsidian's speed and local-first design are beneficial for projects with large datasets or long-term, growing needs. However, for a three-month project, Notion's rich features are unlikely to be overwhelmed. The potential for performance issues at scale is less relevant here, as the project's finite duration keeps the workspace size manageable.

## Trade-offs and Mitigation

- **Offline Reliability**: Obsidian's local files are inherently offline-friendly, which is a strength for inconsistent internet environments. In contrast, Notion requires an internet connection for real-time sync, depending on prior access for offline viewing. **Mitigation**: Structuring work sessions around available connectivity (e.g., using stable networks for initial drafting, revising offline notes during low-connectivity periods) lessens this impact.
  
- **Portability after Export**: While Notion's Markdown exports simplify advanced layouts, the textual and relational content remains intact. **Mitigation**: For a short project, this is a one-time transition concern. To preserve structure, key databases can be duplicated or standardized before export, minimizing any formatting losses.

## Conclusion

For this three-month research project, Notion provides a cohesive ecosystem that addresses the core needs: structured organization of sources and notes, streamlined sharing for feedback, low setup overhead, and consistent cross-device access. Obsidian offers distinct advantages in local file control and offline reliability, but its benefits are best for projects prioritizing long-term portability or low-connectivity use. In this case, Notion's workflow strengths align more closely with the project's scope and timeline, making it the more practical choice.

### 1. Built-in, Structured Organization at the Core
Obsidian is best understood as a *local Markdown workspace with powerful plugins*—but the plugin ecosystem is where the heavy lifting happens (e.g., Dataview, Templater, Calendar, Kanban, Excalidraw).

**Notion** gives you a lot of this *out of the box*, with less configuration:
- Native databases/boards/calendars for sources, tasks, and meeting notes
- Custom properties for author, year, status, confidence, tags, etc.
- Relations between databases, rollups, filters, and saved views
- Nested pages with a consistent hierarchical structure

**Practical implication:**  
For a research project where you're organizing many sources and their metadata, Notion can model a compact literature-review matrix right out of the gate, without stacking plugins.

---

### 2. Single-App Workflow
With **Obsidian**, you can certainly do everything in one vault, but it's file/folder-centric; more of your organizational logic lives in file structure, links, and frontmatter.

**Notion** is designed as a "connected workspace":
- Notes, tasks, project plans, and source tracking live together
- Slash commands, drag-and-drop, and reusable templates reduce friction
- A natural place to keep your project overview, week-by-week logs, and source pages in one place

**Practical implication:**  
For a solo project with a structured timeline and multiple phases, that tight integration can be convenient.

---

### 3. Templates and Low Startup Cost

- Project dashboards
- Research/literature-review templates
- Weekly planning layouts
- Task boards

**Obsidian** has templates and community templates too, but adopting them often means more upfront configuration and plugin setup.

**Practical implication:**  
If you want to hit the ground running with a sensible structure, **Notion** may get you there faster.

---

- **Notion free plan** is very usable for personal workspaces.
- **Obsidian** is fully free for personal use (sync is a paid add-on if you use Obsidian Sync, but you can also sync via existing tools).

**Practical implication:**  
For this use case, pricing is essentially a **tie**.

---

### 5. Sync / Cross-Device Convenience
**Obsidian** stores plain Markdown files locally and you can sync via Dropbox, Syncthing, iCloud, etc.
- Pros: full control, fast local access, offline-ready

### **WeWork**
**Pros:**
- **High flexibility**: Month-to-month is a big plus if you’re not 100% sure a coworking space will stick for you. You can trial it for a month and walk away if it feels like a bad fit.
- **Multiple locations**: Having three spots within 15 minutes gives you room to switch if one feels too busy or if your schedule shifts.
- **Amenities**: Free coffee, printing, phone booths, and event space are nice extras. Phone booths in particular can be a lifesaver for focused work, calls, or when you need to escape the main floor’s buzz.
- **Networking**: The large, transient community and monthly events might be a good fit if you enjoy light social interaction without deep commitment. It could break the monotony a little.

**Cons:**
- **Higher cost**: $350/month is $150 more than The Hive. If you’re only going 2–3 days a week, that adds up to a premium you may not fully recoup in usage.
- **Less intimacy**: A bigger, more transient space can feel less “homey” and more like a hub. If you want a quieter, more focused environment, this might not be ideal.
- **Potential for distraction**: Busy spaces can be stimulating for some but distracting for others. It depends on your personality.

### **The Hive**
**Pros:**
- **Lower cost**: $200/month is a solid value, especially if you use it consistently.
- **Convenience**: A 12-minute walk is very doable and might make it easier to actually go (no commute stress).
- **Small community**: A tight-knit group of ~30 people could feel more like a local hangout. Weekly lunches might be a plus if you like casual community without forced networking.
- **Meeting room**: Having a bookable room is handy for video calls or small meetings.

**Cons:**
- **3-month minimum**: This is the biggest hurdle, especially given your past experience. If you already struggled to use a premium tier before, committing to three months feels risky. What if you lose interest after a month? You’re still on the hook.
- **Past bad experience**: That lingering resentment or disappointment can subconsciously color your whole interaction with the space. Even if this basic tier is cheaper and different, the memory might make it feel like a chore to use.
- **Less flexibility**: One location, one meeting room, no phone booths (mentioned in the amenities). If you need variety or extra study pods, You’re out of options.

### **My take**
For a first foray back into a workspace, I’d lean toward **WeWork for now** here’s why:
- **The flexibility is gold**. You haven’t tried a coworking space in a while, and you’re not sure how often you’ll actually go. A month-to-month lets you test the waters without skin in the game. If you find you love it, you can always commit to The Hive later once you’ve proven you’ll stick with it.
- **The phone booths and event space** are genuinely useful for focused work. If you get distracted in a bigger open office, you can duck into a booth or even claim a corner.
- **You’re not re-stumbling into your old situation**. The bad experience with The Hive’s premium tier is fresh enough in your memory to be a red flag. Starting with a neutral, no-commitment option keeps that over you.

**However, The Hive might be the better call if:**
- You’re confident you’ll use it 3+ times a week and can budget for it long-term.
- You prefer a smaller, quieter space where people know your name.
- The weekly lunches appeal to you as a way to stay accountable and less isolated.
- The $150/month savings outweigh the commitment risk.
- You feel you can leave the past experience behind and not let it sour the new one.

If you find yourself wishing you were at The Hive one month in, you can always commit then with a mindset that’s proven your habits. That way, your decision is based on data, not vibes.

Ultimately, it’s about matching the space to your *actual* needs, not just your theoretical ones. Since you’re transitioning out of WFH, give yourself the room to be distracted at first and forgive yourself if you don’t go every planned day. Flexibility might be worth the extra $150 for now.
